lines: Build a real write-ahead log and a real page, each carrying its own LSN.
Apply the same update two different ways: log the change, then write the page, or write the page, then log the change.
Now crash at the exact same point in both: right between the two steps. Which update survives?
answer: The other update is simply gone, with nothing left to redo it from.

lines: Run it for real: the log-first update survived the crash and recovered correctly.
The identical crash, with the page written first, genuinely and silently lost the update.
steps.takeaway: Log first, data later: the same crash loses nothing with the rule followed, but silently loses the update reversed.

lines: Now replay an already-applied log record against the page it already describes.
Does redo apply it again, or leave the page alone?
answer: The page's own LSN already covers it.

lines: Run it for real: replaying an already-applied record was a genuine no-op, and running the full recovery pass a second time changed nothing either.
steps.takeaway: Comparing a page's own LSN against a record's own LSN is what makes redo safe to run more than once.

lines: A crash mid-write can tear a page: part of its bytes land in the new state, part are still the old ones.
Does a checksum over the page's own bytes catch that?
answer: A half-written page's own checksum simply doesn't match anymore.

lines: Run it for real: the torn page's own checksum genuinely didn't match, and restoring the log's own full-page image fixed it completely.
steps.takeaway: A torn page is caught by its own checksum, fixed by restoring the log's own already-durable image.

lines: One real system's own documentation states the write-ahead rule directly.
Why doesn't a transaction's commit need every data page it touched flushed to disk?
answer: Because the log reaching disk is already enough.
The data pages can be redone from it later.

lines: In that system's own words: changes to data files must be written only after those changes have been logged, and any change not yet applied to a data page can be redone from the log.

That same system's own fix for a torn page is a full-page write: periodically writing a complete image of a page to the log before modifying it on disk, so a partially-written page can always be restored from that image.
steps.takeaway: A full-page write is that system's own name for exactly the fix this topic just measured.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: durability comes from the log reaching disk, not from the page it describes.
That ordering is why the same kind of interrupted write is recoverable one way and simply gone the other way.
A number stamped on both the record and the page is enough to tell whether a change still needs replaying, safely, as many times as recovery needs to try.
And a page half-written by a crash isn't trusted on its own word; its own checksum gives that away, and a separate, already-durable copy is what actually fixes it.
